intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1A) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor (MLR, MR; NR3C2).

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1A) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2).
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the NR3C2 gene coding for the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) cause autosomal dominant PHA1.
checks.explanation: Abstract states NR3C2 mutations cause AD PHA1; mutations detected were heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1) is characterized by neonatal renal salt wasting with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis despite elevated aldosterone levels (Geller et al., 1998). Two forms exist: an autosomal recessive form with severe disease persisting into adulthood, caused by mutations in genes encoding subunits of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), and an autosomal dominant or sporadic form, which is milder and remits with age (Geller et al., 1998). The autosomal dominant form is restricted to the kidney (renal PHA1), whereas the recessive form involves multiple mineralocorticoid target organs such as sweat and salivary glands, colonic epithelium, and lung (Hanukoglu, 1991; Tajima et al., 2000).

checks.evidence_quote: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1) is characterized by neonatal renal salt wasting with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, despite elevated aldosterone levels.
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Hanukoglu (1991) studied 2 kindreds with a total of 9 patients with type I PHA. In kindred I, the propositus presented in infancy with renal salt wasting (vomiting, failure to thrive, short stature, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia) and responded dramatically to a high-salt diet (2.5 g/day); sodium supplementation was discontinued at age 2 years. In 7 additional family members from 3 generations, clinical expression varied from asymptomatic to moderate. In affected members (propositus, mother, and 2 brothers), hyperaldosteronism persisted over 13 years, whereas plasma renin activity decreased gradually to near-normal values, which Hanukoglu (1991) interpreted as the development of tertiary hyperaldosteronism due to autonomously functioning zona glomerulosa. By contrast, the propositus of kindred II, the product of a consanguineous marriage, had severe renal salt losing from age 9 days with increased salivary and sweat electrolytes, recurrent life-threatening salt wasting beyond age 2 years, and still required high salt supplementation (14 g/day) at age 5 years; this pedigree was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Hanukoglu (1991) concluded that type I PHA includes 2 clinically and genetically distinct entities, with either renal or multiple target organ defects.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) studied 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism, a 28-year-old index case in Melbourne and 2 sibs in Munich aged 8 and 2 years, the younger of whom was less severely affected than his sister. Whereas control monocytes bound [3H]aldosterone with high affinity (Kd approximately 3 nM) and limited capacity (150 to 600 sites per cell), no binding was found in monocytes from the index case and the older sib, and the younger sib had 62 sites per cell. Levels in the parents of the Munich sibs, who were first cousins, were normal. Armanini et al. (1985) concluded that pseudohypoaldosteronism is caused by a complete or partial type I (mineralocorticoid) receptor defect and that transmission may be autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Viemann et al. (2001) found no mutation in the mineralocorticoid receptor gene in 2 kindreds with autosomal dominant PHA1 and concluded that autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1 is genetically heterogeneous, involving other, as yet unidentified, genes. Sartorato et al. (2003) found mineralocorticoid receptor mutations in 70% of their familial cases. Pujo et al. (2007) noted that a genocopy may exist in 3 PHA1 kindreds without MR mutations, and suggested that other patients without MR mutations might have different diseases resembling PHA1 in the neonatal period.

paragraphs.text: In 14 families with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) detected 6 heterozygous MR mutations: 2 frameshift mutations in exon 2 (insT1354 and del8bp537), a nonsense mutation in exon 4 (C2157A, cys645-to-ter), and 3 missense mutations (G633R, Q776R, and L979P). The DNA-binding domain mutant G633R showed reduced maximal transactivation, whereas the ligand-binding domain mutants Q776R and L979P had reduced or absent aldosterone binding, respectively, with reduced or absent ligand-dependent transactivation. L979P had a transdominant-negative effect on wildtype receptor activity, whereas G633R and Q776R were thought to result in haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Pujo et al. (2007) screened the MR gene for nucleotide substitutions in coding regions, intron-exon junctions, and untranslated exons, as well as for large deletions, and found a total of 22 MR gene abnormalities in 33 patients with PHA1. They concluded that MR mutations are extremely frequent in PHA1 patients classified according to aldosterone and potassium levels.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Variable expression, from asymptomatic to moderate; remits with age

paragraphs.text: In all affected members of a Japanese family with renal PHA1, Tajima et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous CTG-to-CCG change at codon 924 of the MR gene, resulting in a leu924-to-pro (L924P) substitution. Aldosterone failed to increase reporter activity in COS-1 cells expressing the mutant receptor.

checks.claim: Tajima et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous CTG-to-CCG change at codon 924 of the MR gene, resulting in a leu924-to-pro (L924P) substitution, in all affected members of a Japanese family with renal PHA1.
checks.evidence_quote: identified a heterozygous point mutation changing codon 924 Leu (CTG) to CCG (Pro) (L924P) in all affected members.
checks.explanation: The codon change, amino acid change, zygosity and segregation all match the abstract.

checks.claim: Aldosterone failed to increase reporter activity in COS-1 cells expressing the MR L924P mutant receptor.
checks.evidence_quote: Aldosterone increased CAT activity in cells expressing wild-type receptor, but had no effect in cells expressing the mutant receptors.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly; the experiment used COS-1 cells.

paragraphs.text: In a sporadic case of PHA1, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift mutation, 2871insC, in exon 9 of the MR gene, impairing the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain. Asymptomatic family members did not carry the mutation.

checks.claim: Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift mutation, 2871insC, in exon 9 of the MR gene in a sporadic case of PHA1.
checks.evidence_quote: In the sporadic case we identified a new frameshift mutation, Ins2871C, in exon 9 of the hMR gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

checks.claim: The MR 2871insC frameshift mutation impairs the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.
checks.evidence_quote: This mutation is the first described in exon 9 and impairs the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

checks.claim: Asymptomatic family members of the sporadic PHA1 case reported by Viemann et al. (2001) did not carry the MR 2871insC mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: Family members were asymptomatic and had no mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract says this directly.

paragraphs.text: Riepe et al. (2006) found that the c.2871dupC mutant receptor showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation.

checks.claim: Riepe et al. (2006) found that the MR c.2871dupC mutant receptor showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation.
checks.evidence_quote: The second frameshift mutation (c.2871dupC), which has only recently been reported by our group, showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Riepe et al. (2006) attributed the loss of function of the MR c.2871dupC mutant to a major change in receptor conformation.
checks.evidence_quote: showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous 2157C-A transversion in exon 4 of the MR gene, resulting in a cys645-to-ter (C645X) substitution and a truncated protein.

checks.claim: Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous 2157C-A transversion in exon 4 of the MR gene, resulting in a cys645-to-ter (C645X) substitution, in a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1.
checks.evidence_quote: Six heterozygous mutations were detected. Two frameshift mutations in exon 2 (insT1354, del8bp537) and one nonsense mutation in exon 4 (C2157A, Cys645stop)
checks.explanation: The abstract gives the heterozygous C2157A (Cys645stop) mutation in exon 4. It does not say how many families carried each mutation.

checks.claim: The MR C645X mutation results in a truncated protein.
checks.evidence_quote: one nonsense mutation in exon 4 (C2157A, Cys645stop) generate truncated proteins due to premature stop codons
checks.explanation: The abstract says this mutation produces a truncated protein.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous gly633-to-arg (G633R) mutation in the DNA-binding domain of the MR. The mutant showed reduced maximal transactivation, although its binding characteristics and ED50 of transactivation were comparable to wildtype; the mutation was thought to cause haploinsufficiency.

checks.claim: Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous gly633-to-arg (G633R) mutation in the DNA-binding domain of the MR in a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1.
checks.evidence_quote: Six heterozygous mutations were detected.
checks.explanation: G633R is listed among the heterozygous mutations and is called the DNA binding domain mutant R633. The abstract does not give a per-family breakdown.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous gln776-to-arg (Q776R) mutation in the ligand-binding domain of the MR. The mutant showed reduced aldosterone binding and reduced ligand-dependent transactivation and was thought to result in haploinsufficiency.

checks.claim: The MR Q776R mutant showed reduced ligand-dependent transactivation.
checks.evidence_quote: which is associated with reduced or absent ligand-dependent transactivation capacity
checks.explanation: The reduced transactivation refers to R776.

checks.claim: The MR Q776R mutation was thought to result in haploinsufficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: whereas mutations G633R and Q776R probably result in haploinsufficiency in PHA1 patients
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous leu979-to-pro (L979P) mutation in the ligand-binding domain of the MR. The mutant showed absent aldosterone binding and absent ligand-dependent transactivation, and had a transdominant-negative effect on wildtype receptor activity.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous frameshift mutation (insT1354) in exon 2 of the MR gene, generating a truncated protein due to a premature stop codon.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with PHA1, Riepe et al. (2006) identified a heterozygous ser818-to-leu (S818L) mutation in the NR3C2 gene. The mutant did not bind aldosterone, activate transcription, or translocate into the nucleus; modeling indicated a major displacement of several residues involved in aldosterone binding.

agent.process_note: I read all 12 files in full. Four have only a title and the other eight have only an abstract. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro leaves out the gene MIM number and chromosome location. Hanukoglu et al. (1978) is a title only, so it gives no content on inheritance and is not cited. The Geller et al. (1998) abstract does not name its five individual MLR mutations, so they are not listed as allelic variants. The abstracts do not say whether c.1131dupT (Riepe) is the same mutation as insT1354 (Sartorato), so I did not merge them. No abstract gives a chromosome location, a mapping result, an animal model or management details.
